title: India Ships First Sea-Route Mango Consignment From UP to Dubai, Slashing Export Costs
excerpt: A 12.5-ton shipment of Dashehari and Langra mangoes traveled by refrigerated container from Amroha to Dubai's Al Aweer market, backed by APEDA and ICAR-CISH technology that kept 90% of the fruit market-ready after 25 days at sea.
body:
• India sent its first commercial sea-route mango shipment from Uttar Pradesh to Dubai — 12.5 tons of Dashehari and Langra varieties in a refrigerated container from Amroha.
  • The METWASH preservation technology developed by ICAR-CISH kept roughly 90% of the fruit in market-ready condition after a 25-day voyage.
  • Sea freight costs just ₹13–20 per kg compared to ₹150–250 per kg by air, potentially transforming the economics of Indian mango exports to Gulf markets.
  • The consignment was delivered to LuLu Group, one of the UAE's largest retail chains, opening a scalable channel for North Indian mango varieties in the Middle East.

India has shipped its first commercial consignment of Uttar Pradesh mangoes to Dubai entirely by sea — a 12.5-ton load of Dashehari and Langra varieties that traveled in a 40-foot refrigerated container from Amroha to the Al Aweer Fruit and Vegetable Market, according to Aaj Tak.

The shipment, coordinated by the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research's Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture (ICAR-CISH), marks a departure from the air-freight model that has dominated Indian mango exports for decades.

Why Sea Freight Changes the Math

Until now, mangoes from northern India reached overseas markets almost exclusively by air, at freight rates that have doubled year-on-year. According to industry data compiled by ICAR, air shipping runs ₹150–250 per kg, while refrigerated sea containers bring the cost down to ₹13–20 per kg — a reduction of roughly 90%.

"The freight charges for exporting 700 kg of mangoes to the US by air is almost similar to sending 14–15 tonnes of mangoes through sea route."

— Ekram Husain, VP, VAFA Fresh Vegetables and Fruits Exporters Association

That gap has kept Indian mangoes expensive relative to competitors in overseas retail. India produces about 40% of the world's mangoes but exported only $56.34 million worth in FY25, down 6.3% from the previous year. High logistics costs are a recurring bottleneck, compounded this season by war-driven surcharges and a shortage of refrigerated containers in the Gulf corridor.

Keeping Mangoes Fresh for 25 Days

The central challenge of sea shipping tropical fruit is spoilage. ICAR-CISH addressed this with its METWASH technology, a post-harvest treatment developed at the institute to extend shelf life without compromising taste or texture. The mangoes were processed and packed at a modern packhouse in Amroha before loading.

After roughly 25 days at sea, about 90% of the consignment arrived in marketable condition — a benchmark that officials described as commercially viable. Earlier this year, ICAR-CISH achieved similar results with a sea shipment to Singapore, where Banganapalli mangoes arrived after 16 days with a Total Soluble Solids reading of 20.1°Brix and zero disease incidence.

A Direct Line to Gulf Retail

The Dubai consignment was delivered to LuLu Group, one of the largest retail chains in the UAE, giving UP farmers direct access to a major distribution network across the Gulf. The UAE remains the single largest importer of Indian mangoes, with exports valued at ₹144.41 crore in the 2025–26 season, according to APEDA and the Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics.

Officials said the lower logistics cost translated into an additional ₹15–20 per kilogram for growers — a meaningful premium in a market where Dashehari fetches around ₹25–30 per kg at the farm gate domestically.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian community in the Gulf, sea freight could make beloved North Indian varieties more widely available and more affordable. Dashehari from Lucknow and Langra from Varanasi have long been difficult to source abroad because air-freight costs pushed retail prices beyond what most consumers would pay. A scalable sea-route supply chain could put these varieties on shelves at LuLu and other Gulf retailers at competitive prices throughout the July–August season.

The US market is already seeing a mango boom: exports crossed the entire FY25 tally of 2,188 metric tonnes by mid-June 2026, with APEDA chairman Abhishek Dev noting that northern varieties will keep arriving through July.

What to Watch

APEDA and ICAR-CISH are now working to replicate the sea-route model for other markets, including Singapore, Malaysia, and Hong Kong. Andhra Pradesh and the UAE recently discussed building a dedicated food cluster to create an integrated export value chain for mangoes and other produce.

If sea protocols continue to deliver 90%-plus arrival quality, Indian mango exporters could gain a structural cost advantage in markets where air freight has been the only option. The next test will be whether second and third shipments this season maintain the same quality benchmarks — and whether Gulf retailers commit to recurring orders at scale.
image_caption: Dashehari mangoes, one of the premium varieties from Uttar Pradesh included in India's first sea-route consignment to Dubai. The 12.5-ton shipment arrived at Dubai's Al Aweer market after a 25-day voyage.
